chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
title: Playing alto and hiring Ellington sidemen for record dates
summary: He began playing alto in the section, and used Johnny Hodges, Ben Webster and Juan Tizol on record dates when Ellington's men were restless.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I see. That's a good recap on that. Were you playing alto then, already? Because you mentioned tenor.

No, I didn't. I was playing tenor with Isham, and sometimes baritone, and I was doing mostly clarinet soloing. And then when we started the band, I was going to play clarinet exclusively, and not mess with the saxophone section at all. And I did, for several years. I had a temperamental alto player, it doesn't matter who it was, who gave us a lot of problems, and particularly on one record date or another. And I became a little annoyed and borrowed an alto from one of the other guys, and played a couple of things with the section, and also a solo or something.

And we decided that maybe that would be the best move. And I played some of those things. And in the interim, I had Johnny Hodges come in and do a couple of our record dates, and Ben Webster and a lot of other people, because Ellington's band was -- it was one of those periods with Duke's band where the boys were getting nervous in the band. They were complaining that Duke was taking their backgrounds and making tunes out of them, and a lot of internal strife for that moment. And so they were all -- I would hear from them if I didn't call them about doing some record dates with us. And so we would add them to the band.
How was that relationship between you and
first connected-- members of the Ellington organization, Johnny and Ben and --

Well, it was just because they knew what we were into, and they felt the band was trying something. And whether they agreed that what we were doing was the greatest or not, but they also knew that there was some bread to be gotten, plus the fact that they wouldn't be asked to do something that was foreign to their nature musically. So I think it worked out very well. As a matter of fact, the very first person out of Duke's band that came with us had already left the band, and that was Juan Tizol. And he was the first big complainer about what was happening with the tunes, and there was some kind of strife going on there. So consequently, as I say, if I didn't call them, they would call us and want to know if there were any record dates coming up. And I think that was one of the periods, too, when the band was struggling a bit, in the early '40s.
